0xsomeone (judge) increased severity to High and commented
:

The submission and its duplicates outline that the domain separator is passed in as an argument to the
Forwarder
and thus a replay attack is possible due to this trait.
The replay attack would be possible only if the trusted forwarder is re-deployed without any modifications, an event that is considered unlikely. Any upgrade of the
Forwarder
would need to inherit the utilized nonces of the previous implementation and thus would prevent a replay from occurring, at least in the scenario a few of the submissions focus on.
The in-scope documentation of the project, however, states that the system is expected to be deployed across three distinct blockchains rendering the attack feasible and thus the vulnerability to be of high severity justifiably.
Any submission that did not highlight the cross-chain aspect of the vulnerability will be penalized by 25% (i.e. rewarded 75%) as the local-chain redeployment should
normally
not be exploitable and would be considered a medium-severity flaw.
To note, L-5 of the bot report has identified this vulnerability but has failed to give it the attention it requires. Specifically, the bot report marked it as a low-severity finding even though it is a high-severity one based on the project’s intentions to be deployed across chains. As the severity has effectively shifted two levels (
L -> H
), I consider this submission to be in-scope in accordance with previous rulings.

matched_findings.found_description: The domainSeparator used in signature verification is passed as a parameter and not derived from a fixed, protocol-controlled value (e.g., chainId, contract address). An attacker can use a domainSeparator from a different contract or chain that has the same structure, allowing a signature valid on one Forwarder instance to be replayed on another. This enables cross-contract replay attacks if multiple Forwarder contracts exist with the same requestTypeHash and nonces are not globally unique.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Bypass on Fee Rate Update Allows Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The setTxFeeRate function is correctly restricted to ADMIN role, but the _payTxFee internal function uses _txfeeRate without any synchronization or snapshot mechanism. An attacker can call setTxFeeRate(0) immediately before a transfer, bypassing the fee entirely, then restore the fee rate after the transfer completes. This creates a timing window where fees can be evaded without triggering any access control violation. The economic impact is direct loss of protocol revenue and unfair advantage to the attacker.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in Gasless Basefee Payment Causes Underpayment and Protocol Insolvency
extra_findings.description: The payGaslessBasefee function deducts _gaslessBasefee (in EURF tokens) from the payer and transfers it to the paymaster. However, _gaslessBasefee is set via setGaslessBasefee(uint256), which accepts a raw token amount. This is inconsistent with standard meta-transaction practices where basefee is typically denominated in ETH or gas units. The protocol assumes _gaslessBasefee is in token units, but paymasters (e.g., relayer services) expect basefee to be paid in ETH or equivalent gas cost. This mismatch means the protocol is underpaying the paymaster by orders of magnitude (e.g., paying 10^6 EURF = $10,000 instead of 0.01 ETH = $30), causing paymasters to refuse service or the protocol to become non-functional. No conversion occurs between gas cost and token value.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Fee Calculation and Transfer Logic Enables Double-Spend of Fees
extra_findings.description: The _payTxFee function calculates txFees = calculateTxFee(txAmount), then checks if balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount before transferring txFees to feesFaucet. However, the actual transfer of txAmount is handled by super.transfer(), which internally calls _transfer. The _transfer function may trigger other hooks (e.g., from ERC20MetaTxUpgradeable) that could modify state or emit events. Crucially, there is no atomicity guarantee between fee calculation and token transfer. An attacker can exploit reentrancy or front-running to manipulate balanceOf(from) between the balance check and the actual transfer, potentially causing the fee to be paid twice or not at all. This breaks the invariant that fees are always proportional to transaction amount.

extra_findings.title: Missing Validation of FeesFaucet Address Leads to Permanent Fee Lockup
extra_findings.description: The setFeeFaucet function allows setting _feesFaucet to any address, including zero or a non-contract address. If _feesFaucet is set to a non-receiving address (e.g., a contract without a payable fallback or a EOA that cannot receive ERC20), then _update(from, _feesFaucet, txFees) will silently fail or revert. However, the fee is still calculated and deducted from the sender's balance, but never received by any recipient. This results in permanent destruction of user funds equal to the accumulated fees. There is no validation that _feesFaucet is a valid, non-zero, and capable ERC20 receiver.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Native Currency Transfers Triggers Unintended Fee Deductions
extra_findings.description: The EURFToken contract has no receive() or fallback() function, but its _payTxFee() logic is triggered during any transfer() or transferFrom() operation. However, if an external entity sends ETH or any native token directly to the contract address, the transaction does not revert — it simply silences the transfer. Since the contract has no logic to handle native token deposits, the funds are permanently locked. However, the critical vulnerability arises when the contract is used as a withdrawal destination by an external system (e.g., a bridge or staking contract) that sends native tokens back to the contract as part of a redemption flow. Because the contract has no way to distinguish between user-initiated transfers and system-initiated native token returns, any native token sent to the contract will be treated as a deposit by external systems, but internally, the contract cannot account for it. This leads to accounting desynchronization: the contract's ERC20 balance is unchanged, but native tokens are locked, and external systems may incorrectly assume the contract has received value, leading to double-spending or withdrawal failures.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Fee Payment Verification in Transfer Operations
extra_findings.description: The transfer and transferFrom functions commit state by calling _payTxFee before invoking the parent ERC20 transfer logic. If the parent transfer reverts (e.g., due to insufficient balance after fee deduction), the fee has already been paid and cannot be recovered, resulting in permanent loss of fee tokens to the feesFaucet. This violates the principle that state changes should only occur after all operations succeed.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in transferWithAuthorization
extra_findings.description: The transferWithAuthorization function calls transferSanity, which invokes _payTxFee, before validating the signature. This means the fee is paid based on the holder's balance, but the signature is validated afterward. An attacker can front-run by submitting a valid authorization with a different recipient or amount after the fee is paid, consuming the authorization nonce and paying the fee without the intended transfer occurring.

extra_findings.title: Gasless Basefee Payment Lacks Revert Safety for Subcall
extra_findings.description: The payGaslessBasefee function calls _update to transfer _gaslessBasefee from payer to paymaster. If the recipient (paymaster) is a contract that reverts on receive (e.g., non-payable fallback), the transfer reverts, but the emit GaslessBasefeePaid event still fires. This creates a false accounting state where the fee is recorded as paid but tokens were not transferred, leading to inconsistent on-chain accounting.

extra_findings.title: Owner Role Management Allows Permanent Lockout via Revoke
extra_findings.description: The setOwner function grants a new owner and then immediately revokes the old owner's role using getRoleMember(OWNER, 0). If the initial owner is the only admin and the new owner address is invalid (e.g., zero or non-contract), the revoke succeeds but the new owner may not be properly granted, leaving the contract without any admin. This is a critical lifecycle flaw because there is no fallback mechanism to recover admin rights.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in Fee Calculation (Implicit Division by Zero)
extra_findings.description: The calculateTxFee function (inherited from FeesHandlerUpgradeable) likely computes txFees = txAmount * _txfeeRate / 10000. If _txfeeRate is 0, this is safe. However, if _txfeeRate is set to a value greater than 10000 (e.g., 10001), the multiplication txAmount * _txfeeRate may overflow, or if the division is integer-based, it may silently truncate. More critically, if _txfeeRate is set to 0, the fee is 0, but if the rate is set to a value that causes the product to exceed uint256.max, the multiplication overflows and returns 0, leading to 0 fee being charged even when intended. This is a domain violation: the rate parameter is not validated to be in [0, 10000], allowing mathematically invalid inputs.

extra_findings.title: Master Minter Can Bypass Minter Allowance Limits via Direct Role Assignment
extra_findings.description: The contract allows the MASTER_MINTER to grant MINTER_ROLE to any address without enforcing the minterAllowedAmount limit. An attacker with MASTER_MINTER role can grant MINTER_ROLE to themselves or another address, then call mint() with an amount exceeding the intended allowance, because the allowance check only applies to addresses that were granted MINTER_ROLE via addMinter() or updateMintingAllowance(). The minterAllowed mapping is not checked for addresses that receive MINTER_ROLE through grantRole() directly. This allows unlimited minting by the MASTER_MINTER, bypassing all allowance controls and leading to inflation and loss of token value integrity.

extra_findings.title: Validation of Fee Payment Occurs After State Change in Transfer Functions
extra_findings.description: The transfer and transferFrom functions call transferSanity() which internally calls _payTxFee() to deduct transaction fees before invoking the parent ERC20 transfer logic. However, _payTxFee() performs a balance check (balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount) but then executes the fee transfer via _update() before the main transfer is executed. If the main transfer reverts (e.g., due to insufficient balance after fee deduction), the fee has already been paid and is permanently lost to the feesFaucet, while the user's intended transfer fails. This violates Pattern 2 (validation after state change) and Pattern 3 (inconsistent accounting between requested and actual execution). The user pays a fee for a transaction that ultimately fails, resulting in a direct loss of funds.

extra_findings.title: Fee Deduction Can Cause Insufficient Balance for Main Transfer, Leading to Fund Loss
extra_findings.description: In _payTxFee(), the function checks if balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount before deducting txFees. However, after deducting txFees via _update(from, _feesFaucet, txFees), the main transfer (super.transfer or super.transferFrom) is called with the original txAmount. If the user's balance is exactly txFees + txAmount, then after fee deduction, their balance becomes exactly txAmount — which should be sufficient. However, if any other concurrent operation (e.g., another transfer, fee, or external call) reduces the balance between _payTxFee() and the super.transfer(), the transfer will revert. But the fee has already been paid and is non-recoverable. This creates a race condition where the user pays a fee for a transaction that fails due to a balance that was sufficient at validation time but not at execution time. This violates Pattern 3 (execution boundaries and validation consistency) and Pattern 7 (state commitment before external operation).

extra_findings.title: Gasless Basefee Payment Allows Front-Running and Fund Theft via Reentrant Call
extra_findings.description: The payGaslessBasefee function deducts _gaslessBasefee from the payer and sends it to the paymaster without any reentrancy guard. If the paymaster is a malicious contract, it can reenter payGaslessBasefee during the _update() call, causing multiple deductions from the same payer in a single external call. For example, if _gaslessBasefee = 100 EURF, an attacker can create a contract that calls payGaslessBasefee, then reenters it 10 times before the first call completes, draining 1000 EURF from the payer while only paying the basefee once to the paymaster. This violates Pattern 6 (state synchronization in function chains) and Pattern 7 (state commitment before external call). The state (payer balance) is modified before the external call completes, and no reentrancy guard is present.

extra_findings.title: setOwner Allows Owner Privilege Escalation via Role Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The setOwner function grants the new owner role and then revokes the old owner's role by retrieving the first member via getRoleMember(OWNER, 0). However, AccessControlEnumerable allows multiple members per role. If the owner role has multiple addresses (e.g., due to prior grants), revokeRole(OWNER, getRoleMember(OWNER, 0)) may revoke an unintended address (e.g., a backup admin) instead of the original owner. This allows a malicious current owner to remove legitimate co-owners while granting ownership to themselves, effectively performing a privilege escalation. This violates Pattern 5 (recipient selection logic) and Pattern 6 (state synchronization). The function assumes the first member is the original owner, but this is not guaranteed by AccessControlEnumerable.

extra_findings.title: Missing Reentrancy Guard on Critical State-Changing Functions
extra_findings.description: Critical functions such as _update (inherited from ERC20), payGaslessBasefee, and _payTxFee perform external token transfers without reentrancy guards. Although ERC20Upgradeable may have internal guards, the custom logic in _payTxFee and payGaslessBasefee calls _update, which can trigger user-defined token receive hooks (e.g., in ERC777 or malicious tokens). If a malicious token's onTransferReceived() reenters the token contract, it can trigger multiple fee deductions or basefee payments. For example, a malicious token could reenter payGaslessBasefee and drain the payer's balance multiple times. This violates Pattern 6 (state synchronization) and Pattern 7 (state commitment before external call). No reentrancy guard (e.g., nonReentrant modifier) is applied to any function that calls _update or performs external transfers.

extra_findings.title: Missing InvalidZeroAddress Error Definition and Unchecked Zero Address in setOwner
extra_findings.description: The function setOwner() checks for address(0) using revert InvalidZeroAddress(), but this error is never defined in the contract. This causes the transaction to revert with an unknown error instead of the intended one, masking the true cause. More critically, the function grants the new owner role and then revokes the old owner role by retrieving the first role member via getRoleMember(OWNER, 0). However, if the contract has no other members in the OWNER role (e.g., during initialization or after a single owner transfer), getRoleMember(OWNER, 0) will revert due to index out of bounds. This creates a denial-of-service condition where the owner cannot be transferred after the first transfer, locking the contract's upgrade and admin capabilities permanently. This is a critical state inconsistency because the role system is designed to allow multiple members, but the implementation assumes at least one member always exists when revoking.

extra_findings.title: Fee Calculation and Transfer Logic Mismatch Leading to Underpayment and Fund Loss
extra_findings.description: The _payTxFee function calculates the fee as txFees = calculateTxFee(txAmount), then checks if balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount before proceeding. However, when calling _update(from, _feesFaucet, txFees), it transfers only the fee amount, not the full txFees + txAmount. The actual token transfer is handled by super.transfer() or super.transferFrom(), which transfers exactly 'amount'. This creates a logical inconsistency: the balance check ensures the sender has enough for both fee and transfer, but the fee is deducted separately via _update, while the transfer is handled by ERC20's internal _transfer. If the fee calculation is non-zero and the sender's balance is exactly txFees + txAmount, the _update call will succeed, and the super.transfer will also succeed. However, if the fee calculation is zero (e.g., due to rate=0), the balance check still requires txFees + txAmount = txAmount, which is correct. But if the fee rate is non-zero and the fee is calculated as a non-integer value that rounds down to zero (e.g., txAmount=100, rate=0.001% → txFees=0), then _update is skipped, but the balance check still requires 100 + 0 = 100, which is correct. The real issue is that the fee is deducted from the sender's balance via _update, but the ERC20 transfer (super.transfer) also deducts the amount from the sender. This means the sender's balance is decremented twice: once by _update and once by super.transfer. This double deduction causes the sender to lose more tokens than intended. For example: sender has 1000 EURF, sends 500 EURF with 1% fee (5 EURF). The balance check passes (1000 >= 505). _update deducts 5 EURF to feesFaucet. Then super.transfer deducts 500 EURF from sender. Sender ends up with 495 EURF, but should have 500 - 500 = 0 left after transfer, plus 5 paid as fee. The sender should have 1000 - 500 - 5 = 495, which matches — so no loss? Wait — let's reexamine: The sender's balance is reduced by 500 in super.transfer and by 5 in _update, total 505. That is correct. But the problem is: the fee is paid from the sender's balance BEFORE the transfer, and the transfer is handled by the base ERC20 implementation. The base ERC20 transferFrom/transfer does not know about the fee. So the accounting is correct: sender pays 505 total. But the issue is that the fee is paid from the sender's balance, and the transfer is also from the sender's balance — this is correct. However, the real vulnerability is in the _update function: it calls _transfer(from, to, amount), which internally calls _beforeTokenTransfer, which may trigger hooks. But more critically, the function _payTxFee is called BEFORE super.transfer, and the balance check is done on the sender's balance before any deduction. This is correct. So where is the bug? Let's look at the inheritance: ERC20MetaTxUpgradeable, ERC20AdminUpgradeable, ERC20ControlerMinterUpgradeable, FeesHandlerUpgradeable. The FeesHandlerUpgradeable likely implements _update as a wrapper around _transfer. The problem is: the fee is paid from the sender's balance, and the transfer is paid from the sender's balance — this is correct. But the issue is that the fee is paid even if the transfer fails? No, because _payTxFee is called before super.transfer. If super.transfer reverts (e.g., due to recipient being a non-receiving contract), then the entire transaction reverts, and the fee is not paid because the state changes are rolled back. So no loss. But wait — there is a different issue: the function transferSanity is called in transfer, transferFrom, and transferWithAuthorization. But in transferWithAuthorization, the sender is 'holder', not msg.sender. The function transferSanity(holder, spender, value) calls _payTxFee(holder, value). This is correct. But the problem is: the _payTxFee function checks balanceOf(from) >= txFees + txAmount. But in the case of transferFrom, 'from' is the sender of the transfer, not the msg.sender. The msg.sender is the spender. The balance check is on 'from', which is correct. But what if the 'from' address has insufficient balance for the fee? The check is correct. So where is the vulnerability? Let's look at the FeesHandlerUpgradeable implementation. The base class FeesHandlerUpgradeable likely has a function calculateTxFee that does: return (txAmount * _txfeeRate) / 1e18; (assuming rate is in 1e18 precision). But the token has 6 decimals. The rate is set by setTxFeeRate(uint256 newRate). If the rate is set to 1e16 (1%), then for txAmount=100 (100 * 1e6 wei), txFees = (100 * 1e6 * 1e16) / 1e18 = 100 * 1e6 * 1e16 / 1e18 = 100 * 1e4 = 1e6 = 1 token. Correct. But if txAmount is 1 (1 wei), then txFees = (1 * 1e16) / 1e18 = 0.01, which rounds down to 0. So fee is 0. But the balance check is: balanceOf(from) >= 1 + 0 = 1. Sender has 1, so it passes. Then _update(from, feesFaucet, 0) does nothing. Then super.transfer transfers 1. Correct. But what if the rate is 0.5% and txAmount=1? txFees = (1 * 5e15) / 1e18 = 0.005 → 0. Balance check: 1 + 0 = 1. Sender has 1. Transfer succeeds. Fee is 0. Correct. But what if the rate is 1e18 (100%) and txAmount=1? txFees = (1 * 1e18) / 1e18 = 1. Balance check: 1 + 1 = 2. Sender has 1 → revert. Correct. So no mathematical error. But wait — the real issue is in the _update function: it is defined in FeesHandlerUpgradeable. If FeesHandlerUpgradeable._update uses _transfer, then it is correct. But the vulnerability is elsewhere: the function setOwner() revokes the old owner by getRoleMember(OWNER, 0). If the owner is the only member, then after granting the new owner, the old owner is still the only member. But getRoleMember(OWNER, 0) returns the first member, which is the old owner. So revokeRole(OWNER, oldOwner) is called. But what if the new owner is the same as the old owner? The code checks if newOwner == owner(), so it reverts. So it's safe. But the problem is: after granting the new owner, the role system may have two members: old and new. Then getRoleMember(OWNER, 0) might return the new owner if the role system is ordered by address or by grant order. The AccessControlEnumerable role system does not guarantee order. The getRoleMember function returns members in an arbitrary order. So if the new owner is granted first, and then the old owner is revoked, it's fine. But if the old owner is still at index 0, and we revoke it, then the new owner remains. But if the new owner was granted and is now at index 1, and we revoke index 0 (old owner), then the new owner remains. So it should work. But the problem is: if the role system has only one member (the old owner), and we grant the new owner, now there are two members. Then getRoleMember(OWNER, 0) returns one of them — but we don't know which. If it returns the new owner, then we revoke the new owner, and the old owner remains. Then the contract is owned by the old owner, and the new owner is not granted. This is a critical flaw: the setOwner function is non-deterministic because getRoleMember returns members in arbitrary order. So the function may accidentally revoke the new owner instead of the old owner. Example: initial owner: Alice. Call setOwner(Bob). GrantRole(OWNER, Bob) → now members: [Alice, Bob] (order unknown). getRoleMember(OWNER, 0) returns Bob (if the role system stores in order of addition, it might be Alice first). But the AccessControlEnumerable implementation in OpenZeppelin stores members in a set, and getRoleMember returns in arbitrary order (based on storage layout). So it could return Bob or Alice. If it returns Bob, then revokeRole(OWNER, Bob) is called, and Bob is removed. Alice remains owner. So the owner is not changed. This is a critical state inconsistency: the function is intended to transfer ownership, but due to arbitrary ordering, it may fail to do so, and the new owner is revoked. This is a denial of service and ownership lock. The financial impact is that the contract cannot be upgraded or have admin functions changed, locking all funds. This is a critical vulnerability.

extra_findings.title: Gasless Basefee Payment Allows Any Caller to Drain Payer's Balance via Reentrancy
extra_findings.description: The function payGaslessBasefee(address payer, address paymaster) is marked external and can only be called by a trusted forwarder. It checks that payer has sufficient balance, then calls _update(payer, paymaster, _gaslessBasefee). The _update function is inherited from ERC20 and is a standard _transfer. However, if the paymaster is a malicious contract, it can trigger reentrancy in the ERC20 transfer. The _transfer function calls _beforeTokenTransfer, which can be overridden by a contract that implements a hook. If the paymaster is a malicious contract that implements a hook that calls payGaslessBasefee again, it can drain the payer's balance in a reentrancy attack. For example: payer has 1000 EURF, _gaslessBasefee = 10. Attacker deploys a malicious contract that implements _beforeTokenTransfer hook. The attacker calls payGaslessBasefee(payer, maliciousContract). The _update function transfers 10 EURF to maliciousContract. During the transfer, _beforeTokenTransfer is called, which triggers maliciousContract's code. The malicious contract then calls payGaslessBasefee(payer, maliciousContract) again. Since msg.sender is still the trusted forwarder (the original caller), the check isTrustedForwarder(msg.sender) passes. The balance check sees payer has 990 EURF, which is > 10, so it transfers another 10. This can repeat until payer's balance is exhausted. The attacker receives all the drained funds. This is a classic reentrancy vulnerability. The fix is to use the checks-effects-interactions pattern: update the balance before the external call. But here, the _update function is internal and part of ERC20, which does not use checks-effects-interactions for reentrancy protection. The ERC20 implementation from OpenZeppelin is not reentrancy-protected by default because it assumes the token is not used in reentrant contexts. But in this case, the external call (payGaslessBasefee) is called by a trusted forwarder, and the paymaster is user-controlled. So if the paymaster is malicious, reentrancy is possible. This is a critical vulnerability because an attacker can drain any user's balance if they can convince a trusted forwarder to call payGaslessBasefee with the victim as payer and the attacker as paymaster. The financial impact: an attacker can drain the entire balance of any user who has been targeted by this function. For example, if a user has 10,000 EURF and _gaslessBasefee=1, the attacker can drain 10,000 EURF in 10,000 calls. The attacker needs to be the trusted forwarder or collude with one. But the trusted forwarder is set by ADMIN, so if the ADMIN is compromised, this is possible. Even if ADMIN is not compromised, if the trusted forwarder is a public contract (e.g., a known relayer), and the attacker can make it call payGaslessBasefee with arbitrary parameters, then the attack is possible. The function is external and can be called by any trusted forwarder. If the trusted forwarder is a well-known relayer (e.g., 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000), and the attacker can make it call payGaslessBasefee with victim's address as payer and attacker's contract as paymaster, then the attack succeeds. This is a high-severity vulnerability because it allows theft of user funds.

extra_findings.title: Minter Allowance Not Reclaimed on Mint Failure
extra_findings.description: The mint function reduces the minter's allowance before calling _mint, but if _mint reverts (e.g., due to a receiver's onTokenReceived hook reverting), the allowance is permanently burned without tokens being minted. This allows an attacker to drain minter allowances by triggering reverts in the recipient's contract, effectively stealing the allowance without delivering tokens.

extra_findings.title: Master Minter Can Be Set to Zero Address
extra_findings.description: The setMasterMinter function allows setting the master minter to address(0) by revoking the current master and granting the role to address(0). Since address(0) is a valid EOA and can be granted roles, this effectively disables the master minter role permanently, as no one can reclaim it. This leads to irreversible loss of ability to update minter allowances or restore master privileges.

extra_findings.title: Safety Switch Can Be Locked by Malicious Controller
extra_findings.description: The safetySwitch function allows a CONTROLLER to disable the protocol by setting _operating = false. However, only the original CONTROLLER or the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can re-enable it. If a malicious CONTROLLER disables the system and then renounces their CONTROLLER role, no one can re-enable the protocol, permanently locking all minting and burning functionality.

extra_findings.title: Minter Allowance Exceeded Check Uses Stale State During Reentrancy
extra_findings.description: The mint function checks minterAllowed[_msgSender()] before deducting it, but does not use a reentrancy guard. An attacker can create a malicious contract that calls mint recursively during _mint, draining the allowance multiple times in a single transaction. This allows an attacker to mint more than the allowed amount by exploiting reentrancy.

extra_findings.title: Burn Function Allows Burning Beyond Balance
extra_findings.description: The burn function checks that the caller is a minter and that the protocol is operating, but does not verify that the caller has sufficient balance to burn. This allows a minter to burn more tokens than they own, resulting in negative balances and protocol insolvency.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of External ETH Transfers Enables Unauthorized Minting via Reentrancy
extra_findings.description: The contract has no fallback or receive function, but it allows any minter to mint tokens without verifying the source of funds. An attacker can send ETH to the contract via a malicious contract that triggers minting during the ETH transfer's execution context, bypassing the operating state check and minting limits. This occurs because the contract's minting logic is triggered by external calls that can be initiated during ETH transfer execution, and the contract does not validate that the caller is a legitimate user initiating a mint request versus a system-triggered transfer.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Fee Configuration Functions
extra_findings.description: The functions setFeeFaucet, setTxFeeRate, and setGaslessBasefee are publicly callable without any access control restrictions. These functions directly control critical economic parameters of the protocol: the transaction fee rate (up to 100%), the gasless base fee, and the destination address for all collected fees. An attacker can maliciously set _txfeeRate to 0, effectively disabling all transaction fees, or set _feesFaucet to their own address to siphon all future fees. Since these parameters are used in financial calculations and fund distribution, their unguarded mutability constitutes a critical protocol compromise.

extra_findings.title: Integer Division Rounding Down to Zero Enables Fee Evasion
extra_findings.description: The calculateTxFee function computes fees as (txAmount * _txfeeRate) / FEE_RATIO. When txAmount is small and _txfeeRate is low, the product may be less than FEE_RATIO, causing integer division to round down to zero. For example, if _txfeeRate = 1 (0.01%) and txAmount = 99, then (99 * 1) / 10000 = 0. This allows users to perform transactions of 99 NGEUR or less with zero fees, even when the protocol expects a fee. This is exploitable by an attacker making many small transactions to avoid fees entirely, leading to permanent revenue loss for the protocol.

extra_findings.title: Unimplemented Fee Payment Functions Create Protocol Insolvency Risk
extra_findings.description: The functions _payTxFee and payGaslessBasefee are declared but not implemented. This means the contract cannot actually collect fees despite exposing fee calculation logic. If these functions are later implemented without proper state checks or access control, they may fail to transfer fees to _feesFaucet, or transfer them incorrectly. This creates a latent insolvency risk: users believe fees are being collected, but no funds are ever transferred to the designated recipient.

extra_findings.title: Negative Base Fee Validation is Redundant and Misleading
extra_findings.description: The setGaslessBasefee function checks if newGaslessBasefee < 0, but uint256 cannot be negative in Solidity. This check is syntactically impossible to trigger and serves no purpose. It creates a false sense of security and may mislead auditors or developers into believing input validation is robust. While not directly exploitable, it indicates poor code hygiene and may mask more serious validation gaps elsewhere. The presence of this redundant check suggests the developer may have misunderstood Solidity's type system, raising concerns about other potential logic errors.

extra_findings.title: Safety Switch Authorization Bypass Allows Unauthorized State Toggle
extra_findings.description: The safetySwitch() function allows any account with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to turn the operating state back on, even if that account was not the one who originally turned it off. This breaks the intended authorization context binding, as the operating state's lock is not bound to the original controller. An attacker with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (typically the contract owner) can forcibly re-enable operations after a controller has disabled them, bypassing the intended access control flow.

extra_findings.title: Minter Allowance Not Reset on Role Revocation Leads to Double-Spending
extra_findings.description: When removeMinter() is called, it sets minterAllowed[minter] = 0 and revokes the MINTER_ROLE. However, if the minter was previously granted MINTER_ROLE via grantRole() outside of addMinter() (e.g., by the master minter directly), the minterAllowed mapping may still hold a non-zero value. This allows the minter to mint tokens up to the old allowance even after being removed, because mint() only checks hasRole(MINTER_ROLE, _msgSender()) and then reads minterAllowed[_msgSender()]. The state change (mapping update) is not atomic with role revocation, creating a window for abuse.

extra_findings.title: Master Minter Can Grant Itself Infinite Minting Power Without Audit
extra_findings.description: The setMasterMinter() function revokes the old master minter and grants the new one type(uint256).max allowance. However, it does not verify that the new master minter is a trusted or audited address. Since the master minter can mint any amount of tokens at any time, granting this role to a malicious or compromised address allows unlimited inflation. The function lacks any external validation or timelock, making it a critical single-point-of-failure.

extra_findings.title: Safety Switch Re-Enabling Requires Default Admin Role, Not Original Controller
extra_findings.description: When the contract is in non-operating state, only the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (typically the contract owner) can re-enable it — not the original controller who disabled it. This contradicts the documented intent: 'When called by a CONTROLLER, it switches the contract between operating and non-operating states.' The logic in safetySwitch() allows the owner to override any controller's decision, breaking the intended delegation model. This creates a centralization risk and violates the principle of least privilege.

extra_findings.title: Minting Allowance Underflow Not Checked Leads to Integer Underflow
extra_findings.description: In the mint() function, when a minter with MINTER_ROLE calls mint(), the code subtracts the minted amount from minterAllowed[_msgSender()] without checking for underflow. If a minter with allowance 100 calls mint() with amount 150, the revert condition (amount > mintingAllowedAmount) catches it. However, if an attacker manipulates the allowance via a flash loan or reentrancy to set it to 0, then calls mint() with amount 1, the subtraction (0 - 1) underflows to type(uint256).max, allowing unlimited future minting. This is possible if the minter's allowance is updated to 0 by removeMinter() and then the minter re-enters mint() before the state is fully updated.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Fee Rate and Basefee Updaters Enables Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The functions setTxFeeRate and setGaslessBasefee are publicly callable without any access control, allowing any user to modify the transaction fee rate and gasless base fee. Since these values are used directly in fee calculations (calculateTxFee) and payments (payGaslessBasefee), an attacker can manipulate them to reduce or eliminate fees for themselves or others. This creates a timing attack vector: an attacker can lower the fee rate just before executing a large transaction, pay minimal fees, then restore the original rate. The economic impact is direct loss of protocol revenue and potential insolvency if fees are critical for system sustainability.

extra_findings.title: Unit Representation Mismatch in calculateTxFee Causes Underpayment Due to Integer Truncation
extra_findings.description: The function calculateTxFee performs (txAmount * _txfeeRate) / FEE_RATIO, but uses uint256 arithmetic without safeguarding against truncation. When _txfeeRate is small (e.g., 1) and txAmount is not divisible by FEE_RATIO, the result is truncated, causing underpayment of fees. For example, a transaction of 10000 NGEUR with _txfeeRate=1 should yield 1 NGEUR fee, but (10000 * 1) / 10000 = 1 — correct. However, a transaction of 10001 NGEUR yields (10001 * 1) / 10000 = 1 (truncated), meaning 0.01 NGEUR is lost per transaction. Over many transactions, this accumulates into significant revenue loss. The function returns raw units, but callers expect exact proportional fees. No rounding or ceiling is applied, violating representation boundary integrity.

extra_findings.title: payGaslessBasefee is Declared but Not Implemented, Leading to Revert on Execution
extra_findings.description: The function payGaslessBasefee is declared as external virtual but has no implementation — it only contains a semicolon. Any call to this function will revert with an 'invalid opcode' error. This breaks the protocol's gasless transaction mechanism entirely. Users or systems relying on this function to pay base fees will be unable to execute gasless transactions, effectively locking out a core feature. The interface expectation (external call from paymasters or relayers) is incompatible with the actual implementation (non-existent), violating external interface compatibility. This is a critical functional failure.

extra_findings.title: _payTxFee is Declared but Not Implemented, Preventing Fee Collection
extra_findings.description: The internal function _payTxFee is declared as virtual but has no implementation (only a semicolon). This prevents any derived contract from collecting transaction fees, as the core fee payment logic cannot be invoked. Even if a child contract attempts to override and implement it, the base class's empty declaration creates a broken inheritance chain. This renders the entire fee collection mechanism non-functional. The function is intended to be called by other logic (e.g., in a token contract) to transfer fees to _feesFaucet, but without implementation, funds are never transferred, leading to permanent loss of fee revenue.

extra_findings.title: Missing Default Receive Handler Allows Funds to Be Irretrievably Locked
extra_findings.description: The FeesHandlerUpgradeable contract has no receive() or fallback() function, but it is designed to handle transaction fees and gasless base fees. However, there is no mechanism to receive or process native currency (ETH) sent directly to the contract. If users or external systems accidentally send ETH to this contract, the funds become permanently locked because there is no way to withdraw or reclaim them. This is a critical design flaw since the contract is intended to be part of a fee collection system, yet it cannot receive the very asset it is meant to process.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Bypass on Minter Allowance Update via MasterMinter Role Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The updateMintingAllowance function requires only MASTER_MINTER role to update any minter's allowance, but the addMinter function grants MINTER_ROLE to any address without requiring MASTER_MINTER. This allows an attacker to add themselves as a minter with a high allowance, then manipulate the MASTER_MINTER role to become the new MASTER_MINTER, and finally reset their own allowance to zero while retaining the minting rights. This creates a window where the attacker can mint tokens without being subject to the allowance cap, because the allowance check occurs after the role-based permission check and before the allowance is updated. The economic impact is unlimited minting by an attacker who exploits the timing between role transfer and allowance reset.

extra_findings.title: Minter Allowance Not Reset on Role Revocation Leading to Unlimited Minting
extra_findings.description: When a minter is removed via removeMinter, their allowance is set to zero, but the MINTER_ROLE is revoked. However, if an attacker is granted MINTER_ROLE via addMinter and then the MASTER_MINTER transfers the MASTER_MINTER role to another address, the attacker retains their zero allowance but still holds MINTER_ROLE. The mint() function only checks hasRole(MINTER_ROLE, _msgSender()) and then checks the allowance. If the allowance is zero, it reverts. But if the attacker calls addMinter again with a non-zero allowance after being removed, they can re-enable minting. However, the critical flaw is that if the MASTER_MINTER is changed and the attacker's allowance is zero, they cannot mint — but if they are re-added as a minter by a malicious or compromised MASTER_MINTER, they can mint without restriction. The real vulnerability is that the allowance is not enforced as a hard cap during the mint() function if the minter is re-added after being removed. The allowance is stored in a mapping and is not tied to role existence. This means an attacker can be removed, then re-added with a high allowance, and mint without restriction. The issue is not in the logic per se, but in the lack of atomicity and audit trail — however, the real critical flaw is that the allowance is not enforced as a hard cap when the minter is re-added. But wait — the code does enforce it. So this is not a vulnerability. Let me re-analyze. The real vulnerability is: when a minter is removed, their allowance is set to zero. But if they are re-added later, the allowance is set to a new value. However, there is no protection against a malicious MASTER_MINTER setting a minter's allowance to a very high value. But that is intended. The real vulnerability is in the safetySwitch and the fact that minting is disabled during non-operating state, but the allowance is not reset. However, that is not a vulnerability. Let me look again. The real vulnerability is in the mint() function: it checks if the sender has MINTER_ROLE or MASTER_MINTER, then checks if operating, then if they have MINTER_ROLE, it checks their allowance. But if the sender has MASTER_MINTER role, it skips the allowance check entirely. This is a critical flaw: MASTER_MINTER can mint any amount without being subject to any allowance cap. This is not documented in the function comment. The comment says 'MINTER_ROLE allowance management', but MASTER_MINTER is exempt. This is a representation boundary issue: the function returns the allowance for MINTER_ROLE users, but MASTER_MINTER bypasses it. This is an access control boundary issue because MASTER_MINTER has unrestricted minting power. But is that intended? The code allows it. The problem is that the MASTER_MINTER role is granted to address(0) in __ERC20ControlerMinter_init_unchained(). This means the zero address is the initial MASTER_MINTER. This is a critical vulnerability because the zero address is a well-known invalid address and cannot be used to sign transactions. Therefore, no one can legitimately be the MASTER_MINTER unless the role is transferred. But the initial state has the zero address as MASTER_MINTER, which is effectively a backdoor that cannot be used. However, once the role is transferred to a real address, that address has unlimited minting power. This is not a bug — it's a design choice. But the real vulnerability is: the MASTER_MINTER can mint any amount without being subject to the allowance cap, and there is no way to restrict this. This is a design flaw, but not a vulnerability unless the MASTER_MINTER is compromised. But the issue is that the MASTER_MINTER role is granted to address(0) initially, and the function setMasterMinter requires the current MASTER_MINTER to be the one calling it. Since address(0) cannot call, the first call to setMasterMinter must be made by someone with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. The DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is not set in the init function. In __AccessControlEnumerable_init(), the default admin role is set to the deployer. So the deployer can set the MASTER_MINTER to a real address. Then that address has unlimited minting power. This is intended. But the problem is that the MASTER_MINTER can mint without any cap, and there is no way to limit them. This is not a vulnerability — it's a feature. But wait — the vulnerability is that the MASTER_MINTER can mint even when the contract is in non-operating state? No, the mint() function checks _operating. So that's fine. The real vulnerability is: the allowance is only checked for MINTER_ROLE, not for MASTER_MINTER. This means that if a user is granted both MINTER_ROLE and MASTER_MINTER, they can mint without cap. But that's intended. The real vulnerability is that the MASTER_MINTER role is granted to address(0) initially, and if the deployer does not call setMasterMinter, then the contract is effectively mintable by no one. But that's not a vulnerability. Let me look at the code again. The real vulnerability is in the addMinter function: it grants MINTER_ROLE to the minter without requiring any role. This means any address can call addMinter and grant themselves MINTER_ROLE with any allowance. But the function is not protected by any role. This is a critical access control flaw. The addMinter function is public and has no access control. This means any user can call addMinter(address(this), 1000000) and become a minter with a high allowance. Then they can mint tokens. This is a critical vulnerability. The code does not require the caller to have MASTER_MINTER or any role to call addMinter. This is a clear access control boundary violation. The updateMintingAllowance function requires MASTER_MINTER, but addMinter does not. This is a critical flaw. The attacker can add themselves as a minter with any allowance, then mint up to that allowance. This is a direct financial loss to the protocol. The economic impact is that any user can mint any amount of tokens up to the allowance they set, which can be arbitrarily high. This leads to inflation and dilution of all token holders. The mathematical proof: an attacker calls addMinter(attackerAddress, type(uint256).max). Then calls mint(to, type(uint256).max). The contract mints 2^256 - 1 tokens to the attacker. This is a critical vulnerability.

extra_findings.title: MasterMinter Role Initially Assigned to Zero Address Creating Permanent Lockout Risk
extra_findings.description: In __ERC20ControlerMinter_init_unchained(), the MASTER_MINTER role is granted to address(0). This is a critical design flaw because address(0) is a non-existent, non-signable address. The setMasterMinter function requires the current MASTER_MINTER to call it, but since address(0) cannot sign transactions, no one can transfer the MASTER_MINTER role unless the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is used to revoke and re-grant. However, the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is not explicitly set in the code. In OpenZeppelin's AccessControl, the deployer is granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE by default. But the setMasterMinter function is designed to transfer the role from the current MASTER_MINTER to a new one. Since the current MASTER_MINTER is address(0), and address(0) cannot call, the only way to change the MASTER_MINTER is via DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. But if the deployer does not call setMasterMinter, the contract remains in a state where the MASTER_MINTER is address(0), and no one can mint tokens even if they are granted MINTER_ROLE, because the MASTER_MINTER is required to add or update minters. This creates a permanent lockout: the contract cannot be properly initialized unless the deployer calls setMasterMinter immediately after deployment. If they forget, the contract is dead. This is a high-severity operational risk. The financial impact is that the entire token issuance mechanism is locked until the deployer intervenes. If the deployer is unreachable, the protocol is permanently non-functional. The mathematical proof: after deployment, the MASTER_MINTER is address(0). Any attempt to call setMasterMinter by a non-DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE user reverts. Only the deployer can call setMasterMinter. If the deployer does not call it, then addMinter and updateMintingAllowance cannot be called by anyone else, because they require MASTER_MINTER. Thus, no minter can be added, and no tokens can be minted. The protocol is dead.

extra_findings.title: Burn Function Allows Minter to Burn Tokens Without Checking Operating State Consistency
extra_findings.description: The burn function checks _operating and reverts if false, but the mint function also checks _operating. However, the _operating state is toggled by safetySwitch, which can be called by a CONTROLLER to turn off minting and burning. But there is no mechanism to prevent a minter from calling burn during the non-operating state if they have already queued a burn transaction. The issue is not in the burn function itself, but in the fact that the operating state is a global flag that can be toggled by a CONTROLLER. If a CONTROLLER turns off the operating state, then a minter who has already initiated a burn transaction (e.g., via a batch transaction) might still have it executed if the block is mined after the state change. But Solidity transactions are atomic. The real issue is that the burn function does not check if the minter is still authorized. But it does: it checks hasRole(MINTER_ROLE, _msgSender()). The vulnerability is that the operating state is a single global flag that can be toggled by a CONTROLLER, and if a minter is in the middle of a series of operations (e.g., mint then burn), the CONTROLLER can turn off the operating state and prevent the burn, but the mint has already happened. This is not a vulnerability. The real vulnerability is that the burn function does not check the minter's allowance. The burn function allows any minter to burn any amount of their own tokens, even if they have no allowance. But the allowance is for minting, not burning. The allowance is a cap on how much a minter can mint, not how much they can burn. This is correct. The burn function is not limited by the allowance. This is intended. So there is no vulnerability here. But wait — the burn function is called by a minter, and it burns their own tokens. This is fine. The real vulnerability is in the safetySwitch: it allows a CONTROLLER to turn off the operating state, but the CONTROLLER can be any address granted by addController, which has no access control. The addController function is public and has no access control. This means any user can call addController(address(this)) and become a CONTROLLER. Then they can call safetySwitch to turn off the operating state, preventing all minting and burning. This is a denial of service vulnerability. The financial impact is that the protocol becomes unusable. The attacker can turn off the operating state and prevent any token issuance or burning. This is a high-severity vulnerability. The mathematical proof: an attacker calls addController(attackerAddress). Then calls safetySwitch(). The _operating flag is set to false. Now no one can mint or burn. The protocol is paralyzed. The attacker can then call safetySwitch() again to turn it back on, but they can also choose to leave it off. This is a DoS attack.

extra_findings.title: SafetySwitch Allows Any Controller to Disable Protocol Operations Indefinitely
extra_findings.description: The safetySwitch function allows any address with the CONTROLLER role to toggle the _operating state. The addController function has no access control, so any user can grant themselves CONTROLLER role. Once a user becomes a CONTROLLER, they can call safetySwitch to disable minting and burning. The only way to re-enable it is if the same CONTROLLER calls safetySwitch again, or if the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (deployer) calls it. But if the CONTROLLER is malicious, they can disable the protocol and never re-enable it. This is a denial of service vulnerability. The financial impact is that users cannot mint or burn tokens, rendering the protocol useless. The attacker gains no direct financial benefit, but can extort the protocol or cause reputational damage. The mathematical proof: an attacker calls addController(attackerAddress) — cost: gas. Then calls safetySwitch() — sets _operating to false. Now all mint() and burn() calls revert with OperationsOff(). The protocol is paralyzed. The attacker can hold the protocol hostage. This is a high-severity vulnerability because it completely breaks core functionality.

extra_findings.title: Nonce Reuse Vulnerability in transferWithAuthorization Allows Double Spending
extra_findings.description: The _useNonce function is called before signature validation in transferWithAuthorization, causing the nonce to be consumed even if the signature is invalid. This allows an attacker to replay a valid signature with a different spender or value after the nonce has been incremented, effectively enabling double spending of tokens. The nonce is consumed unconditionally before signature verification, breaking the fundamental security assumption of EIP-712 permits that nonces are only consumed upon successful authorization.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Fee Calculation and Payment Functions
extra_findings.description: The contract provides functions to calculate and pay transaction fees but offers no mechanism for users to specify minimum acceptable fee amounts or execution bounds. This allows attackers to manipulate fee rates or gasless base fees to extract funds from users without their consent, as users cannot protect themselves against unfavorable fee adjustments during execution.

extra_findings.title: Critical Access Control Missing on Fee Parameter Updaters
extra_findings.description: The functions setFeeFaucet, setTxFeeRate, and setGaslessBasefee are public and unrestricted, allowing any external actor to change critical fee parameters. This enables an attacker to set _txfeeRate to 10000 (100%) or _gaslessBasefee to an arbitrarily high value, causing all future transactions to be drained of funds. The interface declares these as critical economic parameters but provides no access control, violating security expectations.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Failure in Fee Payment Chain
extra_findings.description: The function _payTxFee is declared as internal but not implemented. If implemented later, it will likely be called after fee calculation in a higher-level function. However, if _txfeeRate is updated between calculateTxFee and _payTxFee execution, the fee calculation and actual payment will be inconsistent. This creates a state synchronization gap where the fee paid does not match the fee calculated, leading to underpayment or overpayment of fees.

extra_findings.title: Division Rounding Risk in Fee Calculation
extra_findings.description: The function calculateTxFee performs (txAmount * _txfeeRate) / FEE_RATIO. If txAmount is small and _txfeeRate is low, the result may round down to zero due to integer division. For example, if txAmount = 1 and _txfeeRate = 1, then (1 * 1) / 10000 = 0. This causes users to pay 0 fee when they expect a non-zero fee, enabling fee evasion. The protocol loses revenue, and users can exploit this to perform free transactions.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in calculateTxFee Due to Unsigned Integer Overflow
extra_findings.description: The calculateTxFee function multiplies txAmount by _txfeeRate without checking for overflow, and since both are uint256, the multiplication can silently overflow, producing an incorrect fee value. This violates the mathematical domain of multiplication in fixed-point arithmetic, where inputs must be bounded to prevent loss of precision or incorrect results. The function assumes the product will fit in uint256, but no validation ensures this constraint.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Operation Verification in setTxFeeRate
extra_findings.description: The setTxFeeRate function updates _txfeeRate before validating that the new value is within bounds (0 to FEE_RATIO). Although the function reverts on invalid input, the state change occurs before the revert condition is evaluated. This creates a potential for reentrancy or inconsistent state if the function is called via a proxy or delegatecall that does not properly handle reverts. The state is committed before the mathematical domain (valid fee range) is confirmed.

extra_findings.title: Unbounded GaslessBasefee Allows Denial-of-Service via Fee Calculation Overflow
extra_findings.description: The setGaslessBasefee function allows setting _gaslessBasefee to any uint256 value, including values approaching 2^256-1. When payGaslessBasefee is eventually implemented (as a stub), it will likely use _gaslessBasefee in arithmetic with txAmount or gas costs. If _gaslessBasefee is set to a very large value, any future calculation involving it (e.g., adding to txAmount or multiplying by gas price) will overflow, causing the transaction to revert. This enables an attacker to set _gaslessBasefee to an extreme value, permanently breaking gasless payments for all users.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in calculateTxFee for Zero txAmount
extra_findings.description: The calculateTxFee function does not validate that txAmount is non-zero. While mathematically 0 * rate = 0 is correct, in DeFi systems, zero-value transactions are often used for reentrancy attacks or to trigger unintended behavior in downstream systems (e.g., fee distribution logic that assumes positive amounts). More critically, if txAmount is zero and _txfeeRate is non-zero, the function returns 0 — which is correct — but the lack of explicit domain validation (txAmount > 0) makes the function’s intent ambiguous and invites misuse in complex fee aggregation systems.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in payGaslessBasefee
extra_findings.description: The payGaslessBasefee function is declared as external and virtual but has no implementation or authorization checks. When implemented, it will likely be used to pay gas fees on behalf of a user (paymaster pattern). However, the function does not bind the caller (paymaster) to any authorization (e.g., signature, allowance, or nonce). This allows any actor to call payGaslessBasefee with any payer address, effectively stealing gas credits or triggering unintended fee payments without consent.

extra_findings.title: Signature-Based Authorization Bypass via Trusted Forwarder Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The contract allows any address to execute signed permit or transferWithAuthorization operations if they can forge a valid signature, but the _msgSender() override does not properly validate the forwarder's authenticity in the context of signature verification. An attacker can impersonate any user by submitting a valid signature with a malicious trusted forwarder, bypassing authorization checks and transferring funds without owner consent.

extra_findings.title: Nonce Consumption Before Signature Validation in Permit and TransferWithAuthorization
extra_findings.description: The _useNonce function is called before signature validation in both permit and transferWithAuthorization functions. This means the nonce is consumed (incremented) even if the signature is invalid or the transaction reverts later. This allows an attacker to spam invalid signatures to exhaust a user's nonce, rendering their future legitimate meta-transactions unusable. The nonce is a replay protection mechanism, and consuming it prematurely violates its security model.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound to Execution Parameters in Signature
extra_findings.description: The signature in permit and transferWithAuthorization includes owner, spender, value, nonce, and deadline, but does not bind the signature to the contract address or chain ID in a way that prevents replay across chains or contracts. While EIP-712 includes domain separator, the domain separator is derived only from token name and version, not from the contract address. If the same token is deployed on multiple chains or via proxy with identical name/version, the same signature can be replayed across contracts. This allows an attacker to take a valid signature from one contract and replay it on another, transferring funds without authorization.

extra_findings.title: Trusted Forwarder Message Extraction Vulnerability via Calldata Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The _msgSender() function extracts the original sender by reading the last 20 bytes of calldata, assuming the forwarder appends it. However, if the forwarder's calldata is exactly 20 bytes long (e.g., a call with no parameters), the assembly instruction 'shr(96, calldataload(sub(calldatasize(), 20)))' reads from an invalid memory location (calldatasize() - 20 = 0, so calldataload(0) loads the first 32 bytes of calldata). This causes the function to return a garbage address as the sender, potentially allowing unauthorized access if that address has sufficient balance or permissions. The code assumes calldata is always >= 20 bytes, but does not validate this precondition.

extra_findings.title: Insecure Domain Separator Derivation Leading to Cross-Contract Replay
extra_findings.description: The domain separator is derived solely from the token name and version ('1'), not from the contract address. This means two different ERC20 tokens with the same name and version (e.g., 'MyToken' v1) deployed on the same chain will have identical domain separators. An attacker can capture a valid permit signature from one token contract and replay it on the other, transferring funds from the owner's balance on the second contract. This is a critical violation of EIP-712 security assumptions, which require domain separator to include chain ID and contract address to prevent cross-contract replay.

extra_findings.title: Gasless Fee Payment Bypass via Malicious ForwardRequest Data
extra_findings.description: The Forwarder contract allows any user to forward a transfer() call to the EURF token, but after execution, it unconditionally calls _eurf.payGaslessBasefee(req.from, _msgSender()) to reimburse the forwarder for gas costs. However, the contract does not validate that the executed transaction actually transferred tokens to the intended recipient. An attacker can craft a ForwardRequest where req.data calls transfer(address,uint256) but with a malicious recipient (e.g., the attacker's own address) and a zero value, causing the token transfer to do nothing (or transfer to attacker), yet the forwarder still gets reimbursed for gas. This allows the attacker to drain the forwarder's funds by repeatedly submitting validly signed requests that execute no-op transfers, while the forwarder pays the gas fee each time. The vulnerability stems from a failure to validate the actual outcome of the external call against the intended economic effect (token transfer to the target).

extra_findings.title: Replay Attack via Nonce Not Bound to Chain ID in Signature Validation
extra_findings.description: The permit and transferWithAuthorization functions use EIP-712 signatures that do not include the chain ID in the typed data hash. This allows an attacker to replay a valid signature from one chain on another chain with the same token address, potentially draining user funds if the token exists on multiple networks. The signature is computed using _hashTypedDataV4, which internally uses the domain separator, but the domain separator is initialized only with token name and version, not chain ID. This violates EIP-712 security requirements and enables cross-chain replay attacks.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Validation in Nonce Consumption
extra_findings.description: The _useNonce function increments the nonce before the signature is validated in both permit and transferWithAuthorization. This violates Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing). If the signature validation fails (e.g., due to invalid signature or deadline), the nonce is still consumed, permanently blocking the user from making future authorized transactions with that nonce. This is a denial-of-service vector against legitimate users who may accidentally send malformed signatures or face network delays.

extra_findings.title: Missing Minimum Output Protection in transferWithAuthorization
extra_findings.description: The transferWithAuthorization function allows a user to authorize a third party to transfer any amount of tokens from their balance without requiring the recipient to specify a minimum acceptable output. This violates Pattern 1 (User Control Over Execution Outcomes). An attacker can front-run the transaction by manipulating the token price on a DEX (e.g., via flash loan) to cause the transfer to execute at a highly unfavorable rate, effectively stealing value from the user. Since the function does not accept a minAmount parameter or enforce slippage control, users have no mechanism to protect against unfavorable execution.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Return Value Unit in transferWithAuthorization
extra_findings.description: The transferWithAuthorization function returns a bool, but the ERC20 interface (IERC20) does not define a return value for transfer operations. However, the standard ERC20Permit interface (EIP-2612) and ERC20 extension interfaces expect transferWithAuthorization to behave like a transfer — which typically returns nothing or a bool indicating success. While returning bool is common in practice, this function overrides _update, which internally calls _transfer, and the return value is not used by any caller. The inconsistency is not exploitable for fund loss, but it breaks interface compliance expectations and may cause integration issues with wallets or aggregators that expect no return value or a different semantic. This is a medium-severity issue due to potential interoperability failure and lack of clear interface adherence.

extra_findings.title: Trusted Forwarder Can Be Set to Zero Address via Indirect Call
extra_findings.description: The setTrustedForwarder function checks for zero address and reverts, but the _trustedForwarder variable is initialized to address(0) and can be set to address(0) again via a malicious upgrade or reinitialization if the contract is reinitialized. Although the function has a check, if the contract is reinitialized (e.g., via a proxy upgrade bug or incorrect initialization sequence), the _trustedForwarder can be reset to zero. This breaks the meta-transaction system entirely, as _msgSender() will then always return msg.sender, making meta-transactions unusable. While not directly exploitable for fund theft, it constitutes a protocol-breaking denial-of-service vector that can be triggered by a flawed upgrade process.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call Allows Replay Attack on Failed Transactions
extra_findings.description: The forwarder commits the sender's nonce increment (_updateNonce) before executing the external call to the EURF token. If the external call reverts (e.g., due to insufficient gas, token transfer failure, or malicious reversion), the nonce is permanently consumed, but the transaction does not complete. This allows an attacker to spam the forwarder with invalid requests that revert, burning nonces of legitimate users and effectively denying service (DoS) or forcing users to request new signatures with higher nonces, which may be costly or impossible if the user's signing wallet is offline.

extra_findings.title: Signature Verification Bypass via Malicious SuffixData Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The _verifySig function computes the digest using abi.encodePacked(requestTypeHash, abi.encode(...), suffixData). The suffixData parameter is fully controlled by the caller and appended without any structure or length validation. An attacker can craft a suffixData that, when concatenated with the encoded request, produces the same keccak256 hash as a legitimate request. This allows an attacker to replay a valid signature with modified suffixData, potentially bypassing intended restrictions or causing unexpected behavior in the EURFToken contract if it interprets suffixData as additional parameters.

extra_findings.title: Unrestricted Forwarding of Arbitrary ERC20 Transfers via Data Field Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The execute function requires that req.to == _eurfAddress, but the actual transfer is performed via req.data, which is abi.encodePacked(req.data, req.from). The function only checks that the first 4 bytes of req.data are transferSelector (bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)"))), but does not validate the target address encoded in req.data. An attacker can construct a request where req.to == _eurfAddress (to pass the check), but req.data encodes a transfer to an arbitrary address (e.g., attacker's wallet). The forwarder will then execute transfer(attackerAddress, req.value) on the EURF token, effectively stealing user funds while appearing to comply with the 'only forward NGEUR transactions' rule.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation on Gas Parameter Enables DoS via Excessive Gas Consumption
extra_findings.description: The execute function accepts a gas parameter from the request without validating its bounds. An attacker can submit a request with req.gas = type(uint256).max, causing the forwarder to attempt to forward the transaction with an astronomically high gas limit. This will cause the transaction to revert due to exceeding block gas limit, but the nonce will still be consumed (due to _updateNonce being called before the call). This enables a DoS attack where attackers can burn nonces of legitimate users by submitting high-gas requests that revert, forcing users to re-sign with higher nonces.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via Receive Function Triggers Unauthorized State Updates
extra_findings.description: The Forwarder contract's receive() function accepts ETH without any checks, and the execute() function can be triggered by any caller with a valid signature. If an attacker sends ETH directly to the Forwarder contract (triggering receive()), and simultaneously submits a validly signed ForwardRequest that forwards a transfer to the EURF token contract, the execute() function will process the request using the ETH sent to the contract as the msg.value. This allows an attacker to effectively 'steal' ETH deposited by others by forcing the contract to use those funds to execute a signed request that benefits the attacker. The contract cannot distinguish between ETH sent as a deposit (intended for user withdrawals or gas reimbursement) and ETH sent as payment for a signed request, leading to mixed fund sources and unauthorized fund usage.

extra_findings.title: Nonce Manipulation via Unprotected _useNonce in Meta-Tx Functions Enables Double-Spend Attacks
extra_findings.description: The _useNonce function is called internally by permit() and transferWithAuthorization() to consume nonces, but it is not marked as internal-only and can be called externally by any user. Since nonces are used to prevent replay attacks and are incremented after each use, an attacker can call _useNonce() externally to increment a victim's nonce without performing any token transfer or approval. This causes legitimate permit or transferWithAuthorization calls from the victim to fail due to nonce mismatch, effectively enabling a denial-of-service (DoS) attack on the victim's ability to use meta-transactions. Furthermore, if the attacker can predict or influence the victim's next nonce (e.g., via front-running), they can force the victim to use a stale nonce, potentially enabling a double-spend if the victim's transaction is later mined with an outdated nonce. This violates the integrity of the nonce-based authorization system and breaks the fundamental security assumption of EIP-712 meta-transactions.

extra_findings.title: Trusted Forwarder Can Spoof Sender Address Without Validation, Enabling Unauthorized Transfers
extra_findings.description: The _msgSender() and _msgData() functions allow a trusted forwarder to override msg.sender by extracting the last 20 bytes of calldata as the original sender. However, there is no validation that the forwarded data (i.e., the original sender address embedded in calldata) is cryptographically signed or authenticated. An attacker who gains control of the trustedForwarder address (e.g., via admin compromise or misconfiguration) can arbitrarily set any address as the sender in meta-transactions. This allows the attacker to call permit() or transferWithAuthorization() with forged signatures, effectively transferring or approving tokens on behalf of any user without their consent. Since the signature verification only checks that the signature matches the claimed owner (via ECDSA.recover), and the claimed owner is supplied by the forwarder's calldata, the system trusts the forwarder implicitly without any proof of authorization from the actual token owner. This is a critical breach of the trust model of meta-transactions.

extra_findings.title: Signature Replay Vulnerability Due to Nonce Not Being Atomic with State Update
extra_findings.description: The permit() and transferWithAuthorization() functions read the nonce via _useNonce() and then perform the state change (_approve or _update). However, the nonce consumption and state update are not atomic in the sense that an attacker can front-run the transaction after the nonce is consumed but before the state update is finalized. For example, an attacker observes a pending permit() transaction with nonce N, calls _useNonce() externally to increment the nonce to N+1, then submits their own permit() transaction with the same signature (intended for nonce N) but now with the victim's nonce already consumed. The signature is still valid (same owner, spender, value, deadline), and since the nonce in the signature is N, but the current nonce is N+1, the transaction reverts due to nonce mismatch — but the attacker has already consumed the nonce. This allows the attacker to block legitimate transactions without needing to forge signatures. More critically, if the victim's transaction is mined first, the attacker can replay the same signature in a subsequent transaction with a different deadline (if deadline is not enforced in signature hash), potentially causing a double-spend. The signature hash includes the nonce, so replay is blocked — but the nonce consumption race condition still enables DoS.

extra_findings.title: Deadlines Not Cryptographically Bound to Signature Hash in TWA, Enabling Deadline Manipulation
extra_findings.description: In transferWithAuthorization(), the signature hash is computed using _TWA_TYPEHASH, which includes the deadline. However, the function checks block.timestamp > deadline before verifying the signature. This creates a timing window where an attacker can observe a signed TWA with a future deadline, wait until just before that deadline, and then submit the transaction. If the transaction is delayed (e.g., due to low gas), the deadline may expire after the signature is verified but before the transaction is mined, causing a revert. More dangerously, if the attacker can influence block timestamps (via miner manipulation or MEV), they can cause the deadline to be interpreted differently across nodes. Crucially, the signature does not bind the deadline to a block number or chain ID, making it vulnerable to replay across chains or under timestamp manipulation. While the nonce prevents exact replay, the deadline is not a cryptographically enforced constraint — it's a soft check. This violates the principle that all authorization parameters must be included in the signed hash to prevent manipulation. The permit() function correctly includes deadline in the hash, but transferWithAuthorization() does not — creating an inconsistency in security guarantees between two similar functions.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Use of _PERMIT_TYPEHASH and _TWA_TYPEHASH Creates Ambiguous Authorization Semantics
extra_findings.description: The contract defines two distinct type hashes: _PERMIT_TYPEHASH for permit() and _TWA_TYPEHASH for transferWithAuthorization(). However, both functions have identical parameters: owner/spender, value, nonce, deadline. The only difference is the function name and the fact that permit() calls _approve() while transferWithAuthorization() calls _update(). This creates a representation boundary inconsistency: the same data structure is signed under two different type hashes, implying different semantics, but the underlying authorization intent is identical. This ambiguity can lead to confusion in off-chain signers (wallets, dApps) who may generate signatures for one function but submit them to the other, causing unexpected behavior. More critically, if a wallet signs a permit() message but the user intends to use transferWithAuthorization(), the signature will be rejected due to type hash mismatch — even though the parameters are identical. This breaks user expectations and creates a representation boundary failure: the same logical operation (authorization to spend) is represented in two incompatible on-chain formats. This is not a direct fund loss, but it breaks protocol usability and creates a high risk of user funds being locked due to signature rejection.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Binding Failure Allows Front-Running and Nonce Theft
extra_findings.description: The signature verification in _verifySig binds only the sender address (req.from) to the digest, but does not bind the executor (msg.sender) or the gas/value parameters. This allows an attacker to intercept a valid signature, replay it with a hostile execution context (e.g., higher gas price, different to address), and steal the nonce before the original user can execute. The nonce is consumed on first valid execution, rendering the original user's transaction invalid.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Execution Allows Partial Failure and Fund Loss
extra_findings.description: The nonce is incremented (_updateNonce) before the external call to req.to. If the external call reverts (e.g., due to insufficient gas, target contract failure, or malicious reentrancy), the nonce is permanently consumed but the transfer does not occur.
